sh_cinder_oil.name: a cask of Ironbound cinder-oil
sh_cinder_oil.hint: burns however wet the ground gets — Crake, at the trade counter, gives it for the asking

sh_shield_bosses.name: a satchel of dug shield-bosses
sh_shield_bosses.hint: the marks on them want a reader who knows the old tongue

sh_priest.name: Elgin
sh_priest.desc: The field chantry's priest, a man built for patience and worn thin by forty years of it, the chained ledger under his hand the only thing here he'll call finished.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: Elgin, priest of this chantry, such as it is. I've kept this porch for thirty years and buried, in all that time, not one soul from the field behind the ditch.

topics.label: why he's buried none of them
topics.say: Two lines died unforgiven of each other. I will not lay one to rest ahead of the other and call that a rite — either both go to ground together, in the same hour, or neither does. Nobody has ever managed the both.

topics.label: read the chantry's book (wits)
topics.say: The truce-rite's written in here, word for word, if you can read a chantry hand gone soft with age. Go on.
fx: The book gives up its rite slow: a truce spoken whole is spoken for the dead as much as the living, and carries its own words to close it. The third of the truce-words is yours.
The hand's too soft with age, too much of it guesswork. It can be tried again.

topics.label: ask if he'll bury them now
topics.say: At last — the whole field, both lines, in one hour, together, the way it should always have been done. "Thirty years I waited on that," Elgin says, and for once doesn't sound patient about it at all.

topics.label: the field, now the truce is called
topics.say: A truce, whole, at last. I have a rite thirty years overdue to see to, now that both lines can finally go to ground together.

topics.label: the field, now it's given
topics.say: No rite, but no more waiting on one either. The ground's theirs to keep unrited, if that's what forty years of my own failure has finally earned them.

topics.label: the field, now it's burned
topics.say: Thirty years I waited to bury them properly, and now there's nothing left to bury at all. I don't have a verse for that. I've been trying to write one since.

topics.label: ask what becomes of the burned ground
topics.say: Crake already has his eye on the cleared ash for easier digging. I'd rather Harrowfield decided what stands there before his spade does. Your word will carry further than mine.

topics.label: urge a plain marker over the ash
topics.say: He has one cut within the week, plain stone, no saint's name and no side named either. "That much I can still give them," he says, and means both lines, not the ash.

topics.label: let Crake dig the cleared ground
topics.say: He doesn't argue, exactly, but he doesn't come to watch the spade go in either. "Practical," he calls it, the way people name a thing they've decided not to fight.

topics.label: leave him to his ledger
topics.say: Go carefully past the ditch. And come back, if you ever find a way to lay two unforgiving lines to rest at once.

sh_picker.name: Crake
sh_picker.desc: The Ironbound's own bone-picker, knuckles scarred from forty years of a spade meeting old iron, weighing cinder-oil and dug scrap on the same honest scale.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: Crake. Ironbound, for my sins. I dig that field for old iron and sell cinder-oil to whoever's got the coin — and I don't ask what either one's wanted for.

topics.label: digging a battlefield for scrap
topics.say: Four hundred years of iron just lying there, going to rust nobody's using. Somebody was going to dig it eventually. Might as well be somebody who knows what he's holding.

topics.label: ask him for a cask of cinder-oil
topics.say: He hands it over without much ceremony, like he's been waiting all season for someone to finally ask. "Use it well, or don't. Either way I'll smell it on the wind."

topics.label: show him the digging has to stop (wits)
topics.say: Talk an Ironbound man out of good iron? Go on, then.
fx: You lay out plain what every spadeful costs a field that isn't settled yet, and Crake, for once, sets the spade down and leaves it. "...Fine. It'll keep. It's kept four hundred years already."
"Iron's iron," he says, and goes back to the spoil-heap — and the order notes a stranger's petition, tried and lost here. It can be tried again.

topics.label: pay him to leave off (8 gold)
topics.say: Eight gold to walk off a field I mean to keep digging anyway? Convince me.
fx: He weighs the coin twice, same as everything else, and pockets it without a flicker. "Your coin, your quiet. I'll dig the Fallows instead."

topics.label: ask what he's dug up lately
topics.say: "This, mostly," he says, and tips out a satchel of curved bronze, shield-bosses, three or four, marked with cuts he's never once made sense of. "Someone who reads the old tongue could tell you more than I can."

topics.label: read the shield-bosses' marks (wits)
topics.say: Go on, if you can make anything of them.
fx: The cuts resolve into unit-marks, worn but legible: whose levies stood where along the wall, and in what order the line finally gave. Tolan, at the remembrancer's cot, will want this exactly.
The cuts are too shallow, too worn, and you're guessing more than reading. It can be tried again.

topics.label: read the shield-bosses' marks outright
topics.say: You don't need Crake's guess at what the marks mean.
fx: The unit-marks are plain the moment you look for them: whose levies stood where along the wall, and in what order the line finally gave. Tolan, at the remembrancer's cot, will want this exactly.

topics.label: the field, now the truce is called
topics.say: A truce doesn't put the iron back in the ground. I'll go on digging, quieter about it than I used to.

topics.label: the field, now it's given
topics.say: Stopped for good, same as I promised. Forty years of iron I'll never dig now. I try not to think too hard about what that's worth in coin.

topics.label: the field, now it's burned
topics.say: My own oil, in the end. Can't say I didn't sell it knowing what it might be wanted for. Can't say I'm sorry, either, exactly.

topics.label: leave him to the scale
topics.say: Mind your step out there. Some of what I dig up still has an edge on it, four hundred years or no.
